kinds.d: Hydrated copper aluminium phosphate mineral specimen: sky-blue to green nodules, veins and rare crystals; the classic gem stone material (cut stones are under Gemstones).

x.d: Classic Persian turquoise from Ma'dan near Neyshabur (Nishapur), Iran: naturally blue, turns green when heated.
Plain sky-blue turquoise from the Sleeping Beauty mine, Globe, Arizona, mining stopped August 2012; untreated stone has risen sharply in price.
Turquoise from the Kingman mine, Arizona, still operating as of 2015.
Turquoise from the Lavender Pit, Bisbee, Arizona, a copper byproduct often with a chocolate-brown matrix; the pit closed in 1974.
Nevada turquoise with limonite veining forming a web matrix.
Greener, more translucent turquoise from the Sinai Peninsula, among the oldest known mines.
Turquoise from Los Cerrillos, New Mexico, possibly the oldest American mines.
Rare single turquoise crystals from the Bishop mine, Lynch Station, Virginia; first found in 1912.

kinds.d: Calcium phosphate mineral specimen (fluorapatite): hexagonal prisms in blue, green, yellow, purple and pink, with cat's-eye gem forms.

x.d: Fluorapatite crystals in green, yellow, blue-violet, pink or brown; the commonest gem colour is green.
Chatoyant apatite usually cut as cabochons.
Transparent green apatite.
Blue apatite.
Fine apatite crystals from Chumar Bakhoor, Nagar, Gilgit, Pakistan, and near Pech, Kunar, Afghanistan.
Apatite crystals from Ehrenfriedersdorf (Saxony) and Panasqueira, Portugal.
Apatite from the Pulsifer quarry, Mt. Apatite, Auburn, Maine, and large crystals from Renfrew County, Ontario.

kinds.d: Hydrated iron phosphate mineral specimen: transparent blue-green blades and rosettes that darken with light.

x.d: Crystals up to 10 cm from the Siglo XX mine, Llallagua, Bolivia; transparent bottle-green crystals come from the San José vein.
Huge vivianite crystals over one metre long found in mud at Anloua, Cameroon.
Exceptional vivianite from Poopó, Avicaya, Tazna and other Bolivian mines.
Vivianite from the Blackbird mine, Lemhi County, Idaho.
Vivianite from St Agnes, St Just and Kea, Cornwall.
Vivianite from the Kerch and Taman peninsulas.

kinds.d: Hydrated aluminium phosphate mineral specimen: green radiating hemispheres and spherical clusters in rock cavities.

x.d: Green radial clusters from the Mount Ida area, Avant mine and Mauldin Mountain quarries, Arkansas.
Wavellite from High Down, Filleigh, Devon, the first described locality (1805, named for William Wavell).
Fine wavellite from Llallagua and Oruro, Bolivia.
Large rosettes from Bihain, Belgium.

kinds.d: Hydrated aluminium phosphate mineral specimen: green nodules and veins used as ornamental stone; also crystals.

x.d: Former name for Utah variscite, mined at Lucin, Fairfield and Snowville and cut as cabochons.
Variscite from Lander and Esmeralda counties (Candelaria Hills), Nevada.
Historic European supply from Gavá, Palazuelo and Encinasola, Spain.
Marketing term for stones that may be turquoise or variscite.
Variscite from Dug Hill, near Avant, Garland County, Arkansas.
Variscite crystals from the Sapucaia pegmatite, Minas Gerais, and Nevada's Lynn district.

kinds.d: Sodium aluminium phosphate mineral specimen: yellow-green crystals from pegmatites; also cut as gems.

x.d: Discovered in 1944 at Conselheiro Pena and Mantena, Minas Gerais, first thought to be chrysoberyl; described 1945.
Brazilianite from the Palermo and Charles Davis mines, Grafton County, New Hampshire.
Brazilianite from the Buranga pegmatite near Gatumba, Rwanda.

x.n: Paraíba and Rio Grande do Norte brazilianite
x.d: Brazilianite from Alto Patrimônio, Paraíba, and Boqueirão del Parelhas, Rio Grande do Norte.

kinds.d: Magnesium iron aluminium phosphate mineral specimen: azure-blue crystals and masses.

x.d: Lazulite from Freßnitzgraben, Krieglach (type locality, described 1795), and Werfen, Salzburg.
Large lazulite crystals from Graves Mountain, Lincoln County, Georgia.
Fine gemmy lazulite crystals from Chilas, near Nanga Parbat, Pakistan.
Very large lazulite crystals from Hålsjöberg, Värmland, Sweden.
Darker, iron-richer end member of the lazulite series.

kinds.d: Hydrated copper uranyl phosphate mineral specimen: emerald-green square plates; radioactive.

x.d: Torbernite from the Mashamba West mine, Kolwezi, Katanga, Congo.
Type-locality torbernite from the Georg Wagsfort mine, Johanngeorgenstadt, Saxony; named by Werner in 1780.
Torbernite from Margabal, Les Montmins and Brest-area quarries, France.
Torbernite dehydrated to eight water molecules on withering or heating above 75 °C.

t: radioactive: keep in an airtight jar

kinds.d: Hydrated iron magnesium phosphate mineral specimen: bright green tabular crystals.

x.d: Large ludlamite crystals from the Blackbird mine, Lemhi County, Idaho.
Large crystals from the San Antonio mine, Santa Eulalia, Chihuahua.
Ludlamite from Wheal Jane (Kea) and Hagendorf, Bavaria.
Fine crystals from Morococala and Huanuni, Oruro.

kinds.d: Hydrated iron phosphate mineral specimen: pink to violet spheres and crystals.

x.d: Large strengite crystals from Indian Mountain, Cherokee County, Alabama.
Strengite from the Eleonore and Rotläufchen mines near Giessen, Hesse.
Strengite from the Sapucaia pegmatite, Minas Gerais.
Strengite from Hagendorf, Bavaria.

kinds.d: Hydrated iron phosphate mineral specimen: pink to violet crusts and small crystals.

x.d: Large crystals from the Bull Moose mine, Custer, South Dakota.
Large crystals from the Stewart mine, Pala, California.
Phosphosiderite from Hagendorf and the Kreuzberg, Pleystein, Bavaria.

kinds.d: Copper phosphate hydroxide mineral specimen: dark olive-green crystals, named for Ľubietová.

x.d: Very large libethenite crystals from the Rokana mine, Kitwe, and Chingola, Zambia.
Type-locality libethenite from Ľubietová (Libethen), Slovakia.
Good libethenite crystals from Wheal Phoenix, Calstock and Illogan, Cornwall.
Libethenite from the Miguel Vacas mine, Vila Viçosa, Portugal.

kinds.d: Copper phosphate hydroxide mineral specimen: dark green botryoidal crusts that resemble malachite.

x.d: Rich specimens from Virneberg, near Rheinbreitbach, Rhineland-Palatinate.
Pseudomalachite from Kakanda and M'sesa, Katanga, Congo.
Pseudomalachite from Nizhni Tagil and Bogoslovsk, Urals.
Rich examples from the West Bogan mine, New South Wales, and Burra Burra, South Australia.

notes: All 13 planned kinds kept. Handbook of Mineralogy has no apatite.pdf, so fluorapatite.pdf is used for Apatite; torbernite.pdf returned 404 so Torbernite relies on Wikipedia. No brands or traditions. Mexican cave blue apatite not on fetched page so left out.
